title: Probability
description: Class 12 IMO — Probability: conditional probability, the multiplication theorem and independence, Bayes’ theorem, and random variables with their distributions.

topics.title: Conditional Probability
topics.concept:
Conditional probability $P(A\mid B)$ is the probability of $A$ given that $B$ has occurred:

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.$$

Multiplication rule

Rearranging gives the probability that both events happen:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A).$$

Independent events

Events $A$ and $B$ are independent if one does not affect the other:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(A\mid B)=P(A).$$

Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events ($P(A\cap B)=0$) with non-zero probabilities are in fact dependent.

examples.problem: A die is rolled. Find $P(\text{number}>3 \mid \text{number is even})$.
examples.solution: Even outcomes: $\{2,4,6\}$, so $P(B)=\tfrac36$. Even and $>3$: $\{4,6\}$, so $P(A\cap B)=\tfrac26$. Thus $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{2/6}{3/6}=\dfrac{2}{3}.$

topics.title: Multiplication Theorem and Independence
topics.concept:
When an outcome can arise through several mutually exclusive "causes", two results let us move between forward and reverse probabilities.

Law of total probability

If $E_1,E_2,\dots,E_n$ partition the sample space (mutually exclusive, exhaustive), then for any event $A$:

$$P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(E_i)\,P(A\mid E_i).$$

Bayes' theorem

Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning — from $P(A\mid E_i)$ to $P(E_i\mid A)$:

$$P(E_k\mid A)=\frac{P(E_k)\,P(A\mid E_k)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i} P(E_i)\,P(A\mid E_i)}.$$

The $P(E_i)$ are called prior probabilities and $P(E_k\mid A)$ the posterior — updated belief after observing $A$. This is the basis of medical-test and quality-control problems.

examples.problem: Bag I has 3 red, 2 black; Bag II has 1 red, 4 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball drawn. Find $P(\text{red})$.
For the bags above, given a red ball was drawn, find $P(\text{Bag I}\mid \text{red})$.
State the difference between prior and posterior probability.
examples.solution: The prior $P(E_i)$ is the probability of a cause before observing evidence; the posterior $P(E_i\mid A)$ is the revised probability after observing $A$.

recap: Total probability: $P(A)=\sum_i P(E_i)P(A\mid E_i)$ over a partition.
Prior = before evidence; posterior = after observing $A$.
The $E_i$ must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

topics.title: Bayes’ Theorem and Distributions
topics.concept:
A random variable $X$ assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment (e.g. the number of heads in two tosses). A probability distribution lists each value $x_i$ with its probability $p_i=P(X=x_i)$.

A valid distribution

Every $p_i\ge0$ and $\displaystyle\sum_i p_i=1$. This normalisation condition is the first check (and a frequent "find $k$" question).

Mean (expectation)

The mean or expected value is the probability-weighted average:

$$E(X)=\mu=\sum_i x_i\,p_i.$$

Variance

The variance measures spread:

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sum_i x_i^2 p_i-\mu^2,\qquad \text{SD}=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.$$

examples.problem: Two coins are tossed; $X$ = number of heads. Write the distribution.
examples.solution: $P(X=0)=\tfrac14,\ P(X=1)=\tfrac12,\ P(X=2)=\tfrac14$ (since outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT).

recap: A distribution lists $x_i$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum p_i=1$.
Use $\sum p_i=1$ to find unknown constants.

questions.explanation: The sum 7 can be formed by (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). That is 6 outcomes out of 36. 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.q: A random variable X can take any positive integer value x with probability P(X=x) = (1/2)ˣ. The probability that X is an even number is:
questions.explanation: P(Even) = P(2) + P(4) + ... = (1/2)² + (1/2)⁴ + ... This is an infinite geometric series with a = 1/4 and r = 1/4. Sum = a/(1−r) = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.

A letter is known to have come from either TATANAGAR or CALCUTTA. On the envelope, only two consecutive letters 'TA' are visible. The probability that the letter came from TATANAGAR is:
questions.explanation: TATANAGAR has 8 pairs, 'TA' appears twice (prob 2/8 = 1/4). CALCUTTA has 7 pairs, 'TA' appears once (prob 1/7). P(TATA|TA) = (1/2 × 1/4) / [(1/2 × 1/4) + (1/2 × 1/7)] = (1/4) / (1/4 + 1/7) = 7/11.
